label: 1-hour, 100-year storm, change
description: Change in rain in the 1-hour, 100-year storm: short, intense bursts (thunderstorm-type rain: flash runoff, gullies, culvert overtopping)
details: NOAA Atlas 14 (model’s 1979–2005) → 2050–2079 · mean of GFDL-CM3 and NCAR-CCSM4 · RCP 8.5
method: Percent change in the 1-hour, 100-year storm: 100 × (2050–2079 depth ÷ NOAA Atlas 14 depth − 1). The 2050–2079 depth is the mean of SNAP's DOT precipitation-frequency projections for GFDL-CM3 and NCAR-CCSM4 (WRF-downscaled, RCP 8.5; local netCDFs pcpt_<model>_sum_wrf_60m_2050-2079.nc, interval 100), ~480 m cells averaged to the 1 km grid. Atlas 14 is Volume 7 (Alaska), annual maximum series (hdsc.nws.noaa.gov/pub/hdsc/data/ak/ak100yr60ma_ams.zip, 1/1000 inch, NAD83 lon/lat), averaged over 3 × 3 points per 1 km cell. SNAP's DOT depths are Atlas 14 × each model's change since 1979–2005 (Bieniek et al. 2022; SNAP's pipeline uses the annual maximum series), so this is the models' projected change since 1979–2005.
pros: Short bursts grow fastest (median +59 %), as Bieniek et al. 2022 found
Matches flash runoff, gullying and culverts overtopping
cons: Models disagree on the direction in 18 % of land (27 % of the Interior): there the average mixes an increase with a decrease. Accepted as is (an agreement multiplier was tried and dropped as not intuitive)
The two models don't agree on where the change is largest (rank correlation near 0); the average's pattern mostly follows GFDL-CM3, which projects about twice the change of NCAR-CCSM4
1-hour rain from 20 km WRF is a rough guide to thunderstorm-scale bursts
sources: SNAP DOT precipitation frequency, local netCDFs (60m, 2050–2079, interval 100, both models)
author: Joshdpaul
